活塞長笛具有清亮穿透的音色，帶有溫潤的中頻共鳴，介於傳統長笛的輕盈與豎笛的厚實之: The piston flute has a bright, penetrating timbre with a warm resonance in the middle, sitting between the lightness of the traditional flute and the fullness of the clarinet. Its range is wide, and the piston mechanism gives smooth changes of pitch and elegant glissandi; the top register is bright and clear, the bottom mild but strong. Its unusual cylindrical air column lets it overblow the third harmonic, which gives it a rich overtone colour and great expressiveness. Against the nimble lightness of the traditional flute it is more expressive and more jazz-like; against the clarinet it is more open and bright. The way the piston resonates gives it smooth movement between intervals, which makes it distinctive and recognisable in jazz and modern music.
活塞長笛在二十世紀初美國流行音樂、爵士樂與壺樂隊中用作特殊音效，例如保羅·懷特曼: In the early twentieth century the piston flute was used for special effects in American popular music, jazz and jug bands, for example in Paul Whiteman's Whispering and in Louis Armstrong's and King Oliver's band's Sobbin' Blues; it also appears in cartoon scores and television programmes, and in classical line-ups such as Ravel's opera L'enfant et les sortilèges, Hindemith's Kammermusik No. 1, Berio's Passaggio, Ligeti's Violin Concerto and Cage's Music of Changes, and it turns up in Pink Floyd's Flaming and in samples by Deee-Lite.
活塞長笛屬氣鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號 421.221.31: The piston flute is an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 421.221.312, which changes pitch, and makes a glissando, by means of a piston and a duct mouthpiece in the pipe. Folk versions have been found in Africa, Asia, the Pacific and Europe, mostly of bamboo or rattan; the modern version was invented in nineteenth-century England and is often plastic or metal. In the 1840s the Distin family made them and used them in concerts, and J Stevens & Son and H A Ward were early makers as well. In the 1920s it became widespread in the United States, used in popular music, jazz and jug bands; a slide saxophone of the same period sounds with a reed rather than a duct mouthpiece. Its first appearance in notated European classical music may be in Maurice Ravel's opera L'enfant et les sortilèges.

The piston flute (Piston flute, also called the slide whistle) is an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 421.221.312. Its construction is a pipe with a duct mouthpiece like a recorder's at one end and a piston inside; blowing while pushing or pulling the slider changes the pitch, making a rising or falling glissando. Its air column is cylindrical and open at one end, closed at the other, and it overblows the third harmonic. Folk versions have been found in Africa, Asia, the Pacific and Europe, and the modern version was invented in nineteenth-century England. In the West it is often regarded as a toy instrument, but it is common in animated-cartoon sound effects, on Wheel of Fortune, and as a special effect in twentieth-century American popular music and jazz, and it is also used in classical music and in jug-band music.
